analogy.p: The CPU is a kitchen. Clock speed is how quickly each chef works; cores are the number of chefs, who can cook different dishes at the same time; cache is the ingredients placed on the counter right beside the chef, instead of walking to the store room (RAM) each time. Faster chefs, more chefs and a bigger counter all get meals out sooner. It breaks down because chefs can speed up almost without limit if you pay them, whereas a real CPU overheats when its clock speed rises, and some dishes cannot be shared between chefs.
analogy.t: A kitchen in a busy restaurant

bullets: Know the three factors: **clock speed**, **cache size** and **number of cores**.
Know that the CPU performs the **fetch-decode-execute cycle** and performance is about how many instructions are completed per second.
Be able to **explain** (not just state) the effect of each factor on performance.
Be able to compare two CPUs and give a reasoned judgement.
Know that factors interact, so a bigger number does not always mean a faster computer.
Use correct units: **Hz, GHz, KB, MB**.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: OCR J277 section 1.1 asks you to understand that the performance of a CPU is affected by three main characteristics: clock speed, cache size and the number of cores. You must be able to say what each one is and, just as importantly, explain how changing it changes how quickly the computer can run programs. Exam questions rarely ask only for a definition; they ask you to compare two computers or to explain why one is faster, so you must link each characteristic to a reason.

bullets: Performance = **amount of work completed in a given time**.
The work is the instructions of a program being **fetched, decoded and executed**.
Better performance means programs **run faster** or the machine can **multitask** better.
Performance is also limited by other components, such as **RAM size** and **storage speed**.
The three CPU factors are: how **fast** it ticks, how **close** its data is, and how many **workers** it has.
Manufacturers advertise these figures, so you should know how to read them (for example '3.6 GHz, quad-core, 8 MB cache').
core.p: The CPU (central processing unit) carries out program instructions using the fetch-decode-execute cycle. The performance of a CPU is a measure of how much useful work it gets done in a given time, in other words how many instructions it can process per second. A higher-performance CPU runs the same program in less time, so applications open faster, games run more smoothly and large files are processed more quickly. The three factors in the specification each give the CPU a different way of getting more done.

bullets: Clock speed = **number of cycles per second**, measured in **hertz (Hz)**.
The clock produces regular pulses that **synchronise** the CPU's operations.
One fetch-decode-execute step needs one or more clock cycles, depending on the instruction.
Clock speed is sometimes called the **clock rate** or **frequency**.
Example: 3.2 GHz = **3 200 000 000 cycles per second**.
core.p: The clock speed is the number of clock cycles the CPU can carry out every second, measured in hertz (Hz). The CPU contains a clock that sends out a regular electrical pulse, and every pulse keeps all parts of the CPU in step. Modern CPUs run at billions of cycles per second, so clock speed is quoted in gigahertz (GHz), where 1 GHz is 1 000 000 000 cycles per second. A 3.2 GHz processor therefore ticks 3.2 billion times every second.

bullets: Higher clock speed = **more instructions processed per second** = **faster performance**.
Doubling the clock speed roughly doubles the number of cycles available per second.
Programs complete **sooner** and the computer feels more responsive.
Time for one cycle = 1 ÷ clock speed. At 2 GHz one cycle takes **0.5 nanoseconds**.
Clock speed alone is not the whole story: a CPU must also receive data quickly enough to use each cycle.
Exam phrase: 'the CPU can **execute more instructions per second**'.
core.p: A higher clock speed means more cycles are completed each second, so the CPU can fetch, decode and execute more instructions in the same amount of time. If everything else stayed the same, a CPU running at 4 GHz would work through instructions about twice as fast as one running at 2 GHz. This is why a higher clock speed generally gives better performance and why it is the first figure most people look at when comparing processors.

bullets: Higher clock speed produces **more heat** and uses **more power**.
Cooling (heat sink, fan, liquid cooling) is needed at high speeds.
**Overclocking** = running the CPU above its rated clock speed.
Risks of overclocking: **overheating**, **instability / crashes**, **reduced lifespan**.
Laptops and phones usually use lower clock speeds to save **battery life** and avoid overheating.
Link: this is why designers add cores and cache rather than only raising clock speed.
core.p: Running a CPU faster has costs. Every extra cycle uses electrical energy and most of it is released as heat, so a faster CPU becomes hotter and needs better cooling such as heat sinks and fans. If the CPU gets too hot it can become unstable, crash or even be permanently damaged. Overclocking means deliberately running the CPU faster than the speed set by the manufacturer. It can give a performance boost but increases heat, power use and the risk of damage, and it may shorten the life of the component.

bullets: Cache = **small, very fast memory** located in or next to the CPU.
It holds **frequently used** instructions and data.
It is **much faster than RAM** because it is built from faster technology and is physically closer.
It reduces the time the CPU spends **waiting** for data from RAM.
Cache is **volatile**: its contents are lost when power is switched off.
It is **expensive per byte**, which is why it is small.
core.p: Cache is a small amount of very fast memory built into (or very close to) the CPU. It stores copies of the instructions and data that the CPU is most likely to need again soon. Main memory (RAM) is much slower than the CPU, so without cache the CPU would spend many cycles idle, waiting for data to arrive. Cache removes much of this waiting by holding frequently used items right next to the processor.

bullets: **L1**: smallest (tens of KB), fastest, closest to each core.
**L2**: bigger (hundreds of KB to a few MB), a little slower.
**L3**: biggest (several MB or more), slowest of the caches, often **shared between cores**.
Search order: **L1 → L2 → L3 → RAM**.
Going down the levels: **size increases, speed decreases, cost per byte decreases**.
You do not need exact sizes for GCSE: know the pattern and that sizes are measured in **KB and MB**.
core.p: Cache is arranged in levels. Level 1 (L1) is the smallest and fastest and sits closest to the CPU core. Level 2 (L2) is larger but a little slower, and Level 3 (L3) is larger again and is usually shared between the cores. When the CPU needs something it checks L1 first, then L2, then L3, and only if none of them have it does it go to RAM. This layered design gives most of the benefit of fast memory without the cost of making all memory that fast.

bullets: **Cache hit** = data found in cache, so it is supplied **quickly**.
**Cache miss** = data not in cache, so it is fetched from **slower RAM**.
Bigger cache = **more data stored close to the CPU** = **more hits**, fewer misses.
Fewer trips to RAM means the CPU **waits less** and executes more instructions.
The benefit is greatest for programs that **reuse the same data or loops** repeatedly.
Beyond a certain size, extra cache gives **diminishing returns**, and larger caches cost more.
core.h: Cache: effect on performance (hit and miss)
core.p: When the CPU finds the data it needs in cache this is called a cache hit and the data arrives almost immediately. When it is not there it is a cache miss: the CPU must fetch the data from RAM, which takes far longer, and a copy is placed in the cache for next time. A larger cache can hold more data and instructions, so more requests are hits and fewer trips to RAM are needed. That is how a bigger cache improves performance.

bullets: A **core** is an individual processing unit inside the CPU.
Each core can run its own **fetch-decode-execute cycle**.
Single-core = **1**, dual-core = **2**, quad-core = **4**, octa-core = **8**.
All cores share the same chip and usually the same **L3 cache** and RAM.
More cores means more instructions can be in progress **at the same time**.
Cores are different from clock speed: clock speed is how **fast** one core works, cores are **how many** work.
core.p: A core is a processing unit within the CPU that can carry out the fetch-decode-execute cycle on its own. A single-core CPU has one such unit, so it can only work on one instruction stream at a time. Dual-core CPUs have two cores, quad-core have four, and so on. Modern computers and phones commonly have many cores built into one CPU chip.

bullets: More cores = more tasks run **simultaneously** (**multitasking**).
A single program can be written to use several cores: **parallel processing**.
A dual-core is not always twice as fast as a single-core.
Programs that must run **step by step** (each step needs the last result) gain little from extra cores.
Extra cores need **co-ordination** between them, which adds overhead.
Extra cores also use **more power** and cost more.
core.h: Number of cores: effect on performance
core.p: More cores allow the computer to carry out several tasks at once, or to split one task into parts that run at the same time. This is called parallel processing. Running a web browser, music player and virus scan together is smoother on a quad-core than a single-core CPU, because each program can be handled by a different core. However, doubling the cores does not always double the speed, because some programs cannot be split up and the cores must spend time communicating.

bullets: Always consider **all three** factors: clock speed, cache, cores.
A higher figure for one factor can be cancelled out by a lower figure for another.
**Multitasking / parallel software**: cores matter most.
**Single sequential task**: clock speed matters most.
**Repeated use of the same data**: cache matters most.
Other components (RAM, storage type, graphics) also affect real-world speed.
core.h: Comparing CPUs: how the factors interact
core.p: Real performance comes from the combination of all three factors, so a good answer always weighs them together. A CPU with a lower clock speed but more cores and more cache can beat a higher-clocked single-core CPU for multitasking or for programs written to use many cores. For a task that cannot be split, a faster clock speed on one core may matter most. Application type matters: video editing and games benefit from many cores and large cache, while simple office tasks need little of any.

bullets: Clock speed drives the **fetch-decode-execute cycle** (1.1.2).
Cache sits between the CPU registers and **RAM** in the memory hierarchy (1.2.1).
Multiple cores relate to **multitasking** in the operating system (1.5.1).
Heat and power links to **environmental impact** (1.6).
**Embedded systems** use low-cost, low-power CPUs (1.1.3).
Faster CPUs let **compression, encryption and graphics** tasks finish sooner.
core.p: CPU performance connects closely to other parts of Paper 1. The fetch-decode-execute cycle is what the clock speed is driving; the registers and Von Neumann architecture explain what the cores contain; RAM and virtual memory explain what happens when data is not in cache. Embedded systems often use simple, low-speed CPUs because they need only one task, which shows that more performance is not always better.

bullets: Name the factor, **state the change**, give the **reason**, state the **effect on performance**.
Use **'per second'** when describing clock speed.
For cache write about **data being closer / fewer accesses to RAM**.
For cores write about **tasks running at the same time / parallel**.
Write the **unit** and use GHz, MB and so on correctly.
In 6-mark questions give a **balanced discussion** then a **conclusion** for the stated purpose.
core.p: Examiners reward answers that name the factor, say what happens to it, and then give the consequence for performance. A common weakness is writing 'it makes the computer faster' without saying why. Always include a cause-and-effect chain: for example 'a higher clock speed means more cycles per second, so more instructions can be fetched, decoded and executed each second, so the program runs faster'. In comparison questions finish with a justified conclusion.

exam: Command words: **State / Give** = one short fact (1 mark); **Describe** = say what happens; **Explain** = give a reason using 'because / so'; **Compare / Discuss** = both sides and a conclusion.
1 mark: name the factor and its effect, for example 'More cores means more tasks at once'.
2 marks: effect plus reason, for example 'Higher clock speed gives more cycles per second (1) so more instructions are executed each second (1)'.
Never write 'faster' alone: always say **what** is faster and **why** (instructions per second).
Cache answers: 'stores frequently used data/instructions', 'closer to CPU', 'faster than RAM', 'fewer accesses to RAM'.
Core answers: 'tasks run at the same time', 'parallel processing', 'each core runs its own FDE cycle'.
Add a limit to gain a mark: 'not all programs can use multiple cores', 'more heat at high clock speeds'.
6-mark comparison: cover clock speed, cores and cache for each CPU, link to the **stated purpose**, then give a justified conclusion.
Units: write **GHz** for clock speed and **MB / KB** for cache; do not say 'GB' of cache.
Check the question: 'performance' of CPU, not storage or RAM unless asked.
Check marks available and make that many distinct points.
If asked for a limitation of increasing clock speed, answer **heat** and **power use**.

mistakes.r: It can execute more instructions per second, but other factors such as cores and cache also affect overall performance.
mistakes.w: A higher clock speed means the CPU is faster, full stop.

mistakes.r: Clock speed is the number of fetch-decode-execute cycles (clock cycles) the CPU performs per second.
mistakes.w: Clock speed is how fast the computer downloads or loads things.

mistakes.r: Cache is much smaller, faster memory on or next to the CPU; RAM is larger, slower main memory further away.
mistakes.w: Cache is the same as RAM.

mistakes.r: Cache is volatile and holds copies of frequently used data and instructions temporarily.
More cores allow tasks to run at the same time, but not all software can be split, so the gain is less than double.
mistakes.w: Twice as many cores always means twice as fast.

mistakes.r: A bigger cache stores more data near the CPU, so fewer slow accesses to RAM are needed.
mistakes.w: A bigger cache makes the CPU run at a faster speed.

mistakes.r: Cores are processing units, not memory; they let more instructions be processed simultaneously.
mistakes.w: The CPU has more cores so it has more memory.

mistakes.r: It produces more heat, can cause instability and can shorten the life of the CPU.

summary: OCR J277 1.1 requires you to explain how clock speed, cache size and the number of cores each affect the performance of a CPU, and to compare CPUs using these factors. It matters because it lets you justify which processor suits a given job and it is regularly examined as 2 to 6 mark questions.

terms.d: Central processing unit: the component that fetches, decodes and executes program instructions.
The number of clock cycles the CPU carries out per second, measured in hertz.
The unit of frequency: one cycle per second.
One pulse of the CPU clock, which synchronises the operations of the CPU.
Small, very fast memory in or near the CPU that stores frequently used instructions and data.
When the data the CPU needs is found in cache.
When the needed data is not in cache and must be fetched from RAM.
Levels of cache: L1 is smallest and fastest, L3 is larger and slower, usually shared between cores.
A processing unit within the CPU that can run its own fetch-decode-execute cycle.
A CPU with more than one core, allowing several instructions to be processed at the same time.
Splitting a task into parts that are carried out at the same time by different cores.
Running a CPU at a higher clock speed than the manufacturer's rating.
Running more than one program at the same time.
Memory that loses its contents when the power is turned off.

worked.ans: (a) 3.2 billion (3 200 000 000) cycles per second; (b) about 0.31 ns (3.125 × 10^-10 s).
worked.q: A CPU has a clock speed of 3.2 GHz. (a) How many clock cycles does it carry out in one second? (b) How long does one cycle last? [3 marks]

worked.ans: A larger cache holds more frequently used data/instructions near the CPU, giving more cache hits and fewer slow RAM accesses, so less waiting and faster processing.
worked.q: Explain how having a larger cache can improve the performance of a CPU. [3 marks]
steps: Cache stores frequently used data and instructions close to the CPU (1).
A larger cache can store more of them, so the CPU finds what it needs in cache more often (cache hits) (1).
This means fewer slower accesses to RAM, so the CPU waits less and processes more instructions per second (1).

worked.ans: Computer B is better for video editing: it has a higher clock speed, twice as many cores for parallel processing and a larger cache, so it executes more instructions per second and waits less for data. The drawbacks are higher cost, heat and power use, but for a demanding task the benefits outweigh them.
worked.q: Computer A has a 2.4 GHz dual-core CPU with 4 MB cache. Computer B has a 3.0 GHz quad-core CPU with 8 MB cache. Discuss which is better for video editing. [6 marks]
steps: Clock speed: B (3.0 GHz) executes more cycles per second than A (2.4 GHz), so more instructions per second.
Cores: B has four cores against two, so video editing, which can be split into parts, can use parallel processing and run on more cores at once.
Cache: B has 8 MB against 4 MB, so more frequently used data is held close to the CPU, giving more cache hits and fewer slow RAM accesses.
Limitation: more cores and higher clock speed use more power and produce more heat, and software must be written to use multiple cores.
